report:
**Conclusion: the claim is true, with important limits.** In children/adolescents with *treatment-resistant Dravet syndrome*, pharmaceutical-grade oral cannabidiol added to existing antiseizure medicines reduces convulsive-seizure frequency more than placebo.

The pivotal double-blind randomized trial (120 patients aged 2–18) found median monthly convulsive seizures fell from 12.4 to 5.9 with cannabidiol, versus 14.9 to 14.1 with placebo; 43% versus 27% achieved at least a 50% reduction. A subsequent dose-ranging randomized trial also supports benefit. This is therefore strong evidence for **adjunctive, purified prescription cannabidiol**, not evidence that over-the-counter CBD products work or are interchangeable.

The benefit is meaningful on average but not universal, and seizure freedom was uncommon. Harms matter: adverse events were more frequent with cannabidiol, including diarrhea, reduced appetite, sleepiness/fatigue, and elevated liver enzymes (especially relevant with some concomitant drugs). Monitoring and medication-interaction management are needed.

Regulators consequently authorize cannabidiol for seizures associated with Dravet syndrome (with jurisdiction-specific age and co-medication conditions). The evidence applies principally to patients whose seizures remain uncontrolled on other therapy, rather than to all children with Dravet syndrome or to CBD used alone.
